<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span></span></span></span>

<span class="ltx_personname">Pınar Tözün
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id9" class="ltx_text ltx_affiliation_institution">IT University of Copenhagen</span>, <span id="id10" class="ltx_text ltx_affiliation_country">Denmark</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Collocating deep learning training tasks improves GPU utilization but causes drastic slowdowns due to resource contention and risks Out-of-Memory (OOM) failures. Accurate memory estimation is essential for robust collocation, while GPU utilization — a key proxy for resource contention — enables interference-aware scheduling to reduce slowdowns and improve throughput. Existing GPU memory estimators span three paradigms — analytical models, CPU-side libraries, and ML-based estimators — each with distinct limitations: dependence on detailed model specifications, intrusive integration, poor generalization, and varying latency overhead. GPU heterogeneity further complicates estimation, as identical tasks can exhibit markedly different memory footprints across hardware generations. GPU utilization remains comparatively understudied, further complicated by the non-additive nature of utilization metrics and hardware sensitivity.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We conduct a systematic analysis of representative estimators from each paradigm — Horus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeung et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, PyTorch FakeTensor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite>, and our lightweight ML-based estimator — evaluating accuracy, generalizability, and practical overhead. We construct a synthetic dataset spanning MLPs, CNNs, and Transformers with controlled architectural variations, and train MLP- and Transformer-based estimators for memory prediction. We further experiment with utilization estimation on the same dataset. Our evaluation reveals key tradeoffs and validates estimators against real-world unseen models. Significant challenges remain: analytical models are hardware-dependent, CPU-side libraries impose intrusive integration costs, and ML-based estimators struggle with cross-architecture generalization. We release all datasets, tools, and artifacts to support further research.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Accurate GPU memory estimation is critical for robust resource management in deep learning workloads, enabling appropriate GPU selection and safe task collocation without exceeding memory limits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Robroek et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Estimating related metrics such as GPU utilization, as a proxy for interference, and memory bandwidth can further optimize collocation decisions and reduce performance degradations because of resource contention. However, estimation introduces latency into the critical path of resource manager decision-making, necessitating fast estimation methods, offloading to machine learning frameworks during development, or pre-computation before tasks reach the mapper component.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Deep learning training tasks are compute-intensive and demand substantial GPU memory based on model architecture, model size, input data size, and batch size, making efficient memory management essential. Maximizing GPU utilization is also necessary for energy efficiency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeon et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weng et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Modern frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paszke et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abadi et al., 2016</a>)</cite> employ optimization techniques like <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">activation reuse</span> and <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dynamic allocation</span>, introducing unpredictability into memory usage patterns of training tasks. Consequently, simple estimation formulas based solely on numbers of parameters, gradients and activations often fail to produce accurate predictions. This complexity is further compounded by the fact that identical training tasks can exhibit markedly different memory footprints across different GPU hardware models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Albahar et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, owing to differences in software stacks, and hardware architecture as discussed in Section <a href="#S2" title="2. Related Work ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Beyond memory, GPU utilization estimation faces distinct challenges: hardware heterogeneity causes the same task to exhibit different utilization across GPU architectures, and utilization metrics are <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">non-additive</span>, complicating collocation decisions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing GPU memory estimation approaches — spanning analytical methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeung et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, library-based CPU-side tools <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and ML-based estimators <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> — universally suffer from over- or underestimation, dependence on detailed model specifications or computation graph, poor generalizability, and latency overhead on the critical scheduling/mapping path. GPU utilization estimation remains comparatively understudied, despite its controversial interpretation as a proxy for interference-aware collocation. Reactive and/or profiling-based collocation systems such as Gandiva <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, Gavel <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Narayanan et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and Orion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Strati et al., 2024</a>)</cite> each address interference management under different assumptions, yet share fundamental limitations in intrusiveness, scheduling granularity, or profiling overhead. These challenges can further get compounded if workloads show a change in their behavior, where memory consumption and GPU utilization can shift substantially over a job’s execution lifetime.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we analyze existing GPU memory and utilization estimators, expose their practical limitations, and also release <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPUMemNet</span> and <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPUUtilNet<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">1</span></span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <span id="footnote1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">All artifacts, datasets, and reproducibility scripts are publicly available at </span><a href="https://github.com/itu-rad/GPUMemNet" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">https://github.com/itu-rad/GPUMemNet</a><span id="footnote1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> and </span><a href="https://github.com/itu-rad/GPUUtilNet" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">https://github.com/itu-rad/GPUUtilNet</a><span id="footnote1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">.</span></span></span></span></span>, deep learning-based estimators for GPU memory consumption and utilization metrics respectively, achieving up to 97% estimation accuracy for MLPs and 82–87% for CNN and Transformer models, with limited generalization to real-world architectures such as ResNet, EfficientNet, and BERT.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.p5.2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We organize existing GPU memory estimation methods into three categories — analytical, library-based, and ML-based — and provide a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative comparison of representative techniques from each class: Horus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeung et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, PyTorch FakeTensor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite>, and our own <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPUMemNet</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPUMemNet</span> and <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPUUtilNet</span>, together with a fully reproducible estimation pipeline encompassing data generation scripts for MLP, CNN, and Transformer architectures, curated training datasets, and documented Jupyter notebooks, lowering the barrier for the community to extend and build upon our work.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide a structured discussion of the key challenges, open limitations, and future directions in GPU memory and utilization estimation, with an emphasis on their implications for collocation and resource management in shared GPU clusters.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: <a href="#S2" title="2. Related Work ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reviews literature on GPU resource estimation and interference mitigation. <a href="#S3" title="3. Selected Estimators for This Study ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> details the selected estimators, while <a href="#S4" title="4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> describes the dataset collection, problem formulation, feature engineering. <a href="#S5" title="5. Methodology ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> outlines the experimental setup, followed by a performance analysis in <a href="#S6" title="6. Evaluation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. Finally, <a href="#S7" title="7. Discussion and Limitations ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> discusses limitations and future work, with concluding remarks in <a href="#S8" title="8. Conclusion ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPU resource estimation and GPU resource management, specifically collocation management have received growing attention as shared GPU clusters suffer from underutilization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeon et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weng et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. We organize the related literature along two axes: <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">static estimation</span> approaches that predict memory and utilization prior to execution, and <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">online, reactive</span> approaches that manage interference dynamically during collocation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1. </span>GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Approaches to GPU memory estimation fall into three broad categories.
Analytical methods derive memory estimates from model structure using closed-form accounting. Horus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeung et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and DNNMem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2020</a>)</cite> are representative of this class; both require detailed architectural specifications and exhibit limited adaptability to transformer-based models and multi-GPU configurations, with DNNMem further lacking a publicly available implementation. LLMem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite> extends the analytical paradigm to distributed LLM fine-tuning, achieving low error rates, but remains tightly coupled to transformer decoder architectures, precluding generalization to other model families.
Library-based CPU-side tools perform symbolic or formula-driven estimation without executing the model.
xMem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2025</a>)</cite> utilizes the CPU to execute the initial iterations of a target task for a brief period to gather the necessary data for its estimation process. During this CPU execution, it collects detailed execution traces, including memory events and operator calls, allowing it to estimate peak memory requirements without needing a GPU.
PyTorch FakeTensor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite> propagates tensor shapes symbolically to estimate memory, while DeepSpeed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Microsoft DeepSpeed Team, 2023</a>)</cite> provides built-in estimation utilities scoped to ZeRO-stage configurations; both require access to model source code or parameter counts and fail to account for framework-level overhead such as activation memory, gradient checkpointing, and caching allocator reservations. ML-based approaches attempt to overcome the rigidity of analytical methods; DNNPerf <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> employs graph neural networks to improve prediction accuracy, though it demands substantial computational resources and struggles to generalize to architectures unseen during training. Despite spanning three distinct paradigms, all methods share fundamental shortcomings: dependence on detailed model specifications or architecture internals, poor extensibility to unseen model families, and non-negligible inference latency that burdens the critical scheduling path. GPU utilization estimation remains comparatively understudied; Horus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeung et al., 2022</a>)</cite> is among the few works to address it, yet its reliance on a small, curated model dataset limits its applicability to the diverse workloads encountered in production clusters.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2. </span>Collocation and Interference Management</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Online, reactive approaches have been proposed to manage interference that arises when multiple training jobs share a GPU. Gandiva <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2018</a>)</cite> supports collocation through time-slicing and introspective profiling of mini-batch progress rates, reverting packing decisions when significant slowdown is detected; however, this requires tight co-design between the ML framework and the resource manager, introducing substantial system intrusiveness. Gavel <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Narayanan et al., 2020</a>)</cite> adopts a round-based scheduling mechanism with a fixed round length to make heterogeneity-aware allocation decisions, but a static round granularity is inherently ill-suited for workloads with widely varying iteration times — too coarse for short jobs and too fine for long ones. Orion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Strati et al., 2024</a>)</cite> achieves fine-grained, kernel-level collocation on a single GPU by classifying kernels as compute- or memory-bound through extensive offline profiling and intercepting kernel launches via an additional layer in the software stack; while effective, this approach incurs heavy profiling overhead and adds architectural complexity that hinders broader deployment.
A common thread across these systems is that they treat interference reactively, after collocation has already been established, rather than proactively avoiding it through accurate pre-execution estimation. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of training workloads — where memory consumption and GPU utilization can shift substantially over the course of a job’s execution lifetime — remains largely unaddressed across both estimation and collocation literature, and we identify this as a critical frontier for future investigation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Selected Estimators for This Study</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>GPU Memory Estimators</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the three classes of GPU memory estimators surveyed above, we select one available method per paradigm for empirical evaluation, the Horus analytical formula <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeung et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, PyTorch FakeTensor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite>, and our own lightweight ML-based estimator, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPUMemNet</span>. The reason for excluded estimators, for instance, DNNMem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, which is not publicly available, LLMem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which is restricted to transformer decoder fine-tuning, and DeepSpeed’s estimator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Microsoft DeepSpeed Team, 2023</a>)</cite>, which is scoped exclusively to ZeRO-stage configurations and does not account for activation memory or framework overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analytical.</span>
The Horus formula <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeung et al., 2022</a>)</cite> estimates training memory via a lightweight analytical pass over model statistics, incurring negligible runtime overhead. However, as we demonstrate in <a href="#S3.F1" title="In 3.1. GPU Memory Estimators ‣ 3. Selected Estimators for This Study ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, it systematically overestimates memory consumption across MLP configurations due to its inability to account for framework-level optimizations such as activation reuse, dynamic memory management, and layer fusion. While this conservatism avoids OOM failures, it unnecessarily reduces collocation opportunities by over-reserving memory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FakeTensor.</span>
PyTorch FakeTensor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite> performs symbolic shape propagation, creating lightweight tensor surrogates that carry metadata — shape, dtype, device — without allocating real memory. This allows it to trace model execution and estimate memory without instrumentation of the training process itself. Evaluated across 2,030 model configurations from the <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TIMM</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wightman, 2019</a>)</cite> library, FakeTensor consistently <em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">underestimates</em> peak memory usage (<a href="#S3.T1" title="In 3.1. GPU Memory Estimators ‣ 3. Selected Estimators for This Study ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), as it does not account for the caching allocator’s reserved memory, intermediate buffers, or optimizer states. A fixed safety margin (e.g., <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">+4,GB</span>) can partially compensate for this, providing a conservative bound suitable for collocation decisions. Its runtime overhead, while modest, is the most prominent among the three candidates and adds latency to the scheduling critical path. Additionally, FakeTensor fails on architectures that rely on unsupported operations, dynamic control flow, or CUDA-only kernels — including many Transformer variants, DLRM, and Mask R-CNN — limiting its practical coverage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ML-based estimator</span>
<span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPUMemNet</span>, our ML-based estimator, is trained on a curated synthetic dataset spanning MLP, CNN, and Transformer architecture families and formulates memory prediction as a classification task over discretized memory ranges. Unlike the analytical and library-based alternatives, it requires no model source code, no architectural specification beyond high-level configuration parameters, and introduces minimal inference latency. Its limitations and generalization behavior are analyzed in detail in <a href="#S6" title="6. Evaluation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17817v1/horus_formula_not_working.png" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/203;" width="476" height="203" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Actual GPU memory need vs Horus’ estimations for MLP models with varying number of neurons and layers.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>GPU Utilization Estimator</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given that GPU utilization metrics remain largely understudied and the Horus dataset and models are currently unavailable, we propose a deep learning-based estimator for utilization metrics—specifically SMACT, SMOCC, and DRAMA—trained on the dataset we curated for GPU memory estimation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4. </span>Dataset and Problem Formulation</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section presents the curated dataset, covering data collection, processing, analysis, and the training and testing pipeline. We first outline the scripts and key considerations for constructing a valid dataset (<a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1. Data Collection, Processing, Analysis, and Training Pipeline ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>), then justify the formulation of GPU memory and utilization estimation as a classification task (<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2. Classification vs. Regression. ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>). We evaluated models of increasing complexity—from tree-based regressors to MLP- and Transformer-based architectures—using the latter to examine how layer sequences, activations, and parameters influence estimation performance. Finally, we describe the dataset and selected features for the MLP- and Transformer-based estimators (<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3. Selected Features ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1. </span>Data Collection, Processing, Analysis, and Training Pipeline</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To systematically collect GPU memory usage data, we developed a suite of scripts tailored to three different neural network architecture families: <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MLPs</span>, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CNNs</span>, and <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transformers</span>. For each architecture, two main scripts are implemented:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(1)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Configurable Model Script:</span> 
<br class="ltx_break">This script defines a configurable neural network, supporting a flexible range of hyperparameters and architectural topologies (e.g., pyramid, hourglass, etc.). It ensures that only valid model configurations—feasible in terms of depth, width, and architecture—are generated. This validation guarantees the practicality of the network in real-world settings.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(2)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Launcher Script:</span> 
<br class="ltx_break">The launcher orchestrates data collection by uniformly sampling hyperparameters from predefined ranges. It launches a fixed number of configurations per run, with each configuration representing a unique data point. The parameters can be tweeked within the corresponding yaml file. <a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.1. Data Collection, Processing, Analysis, and Training Pipeline ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows inside the yaml file for MLP data collection. After configuring the parameters, running the script with <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">python launcher_mlp.py</span>, the data collection starts. The same goes for the two other as well.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S4.F2.3" class="ltx_listing ltx_lst_language_yaml ltx_lst_numbers_left ltx_lstlisting ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing" style="width:345.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:#F9F9F9;"><div class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64,YmFzZV9kYXRhX2RpcjogIm1scF9kYXRhc2V0IgpudW1fcmFuZG9tX2NvbmZpZ3M6IDMwMDAgIyBudW1iZXIgb2YgZGF0YSBwb2ludHMKaW5wdXRfc2l6ZToKICBtaW46IDQKICBtYXg6IDQwOTYKb3V0cHV0X3NpemU6CiAgbWluX3JhdGlvOiAwLjI1CmJhdGNoX3NpemU6CiAgbWluOiAxCiAgbWF4OiAyNTYKLi4u" download="">⬇</a></div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>. </span><span id="S4.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">YAML configuration for MLP generation</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Each generated model is trained for a fixed, configurable duration of one minute, during which GPU and system resources are monitored via <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">nvidia-smi<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">(</span><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Corporation, [n. d.]</a><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">)</span></cite></span>, <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">dcgmi<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">(</span><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Corporation, 2024</a><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">)</span></cite></span>, and <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">top</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Documentation, [n. d.]</a>)</cite>. These tools capture GPU memory usage, utilization metrics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yousefzadeh-Asl-Miandoab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, power consumption, CPU load, and RAM usage. All raw monitoring logs and the model’s architectural summary are saved in dedicated per-configuration directories.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1. </span>Data Cleaning and Feature Extraction</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each architecture type, a specialized <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">data cleaner script</span> parses the corresponding logs and summary files. These scripts extract:</p>
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model-specific features (e.g., number of different layers, total parameters, depth-width profiles)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Runtime GPU metrics (e.g., peak memory usage, utilization)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">System metrics (e.g., CPU%, MEM%)</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The cleaned and structured datasets are saved in a standardized format for seamless downstream processing. While the primary targets are GPU memory usage and utilization metrics (SMACT, SMOCC, DRAMA), the pipeline preserves a broad set of features to support future research directions, such as energy consumption or latency prediction. Data cleaning scripts are configured by specifying the raw dataset directory and the desired output CSV path.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2. </span>Analysis and Modeling</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Subsequent analysis is performed through detailed <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Jupyter Notebooks</span>, included in the repository. These notebooks:</p>
<ul id="S4.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Visualize the collected data and distributions</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Provide a step-by-step guide for training memory usage estimators using MLP-based and Transformer-based models</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Include preprocessing, training, and evaluation logic</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.3. </span>Estimator Training and Evaluation</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement and evaluate <span id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ensemble-based estimators</span> for memory usage prediction. Each ensemble aggregates multiple base models with varied hyperparameters and structures to improve generalization. Models are trained and evaluated using <span id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3-fold cross-validation</span>, ensuring robust performance reporting across all architecture families.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.4. </span>Testing on unseen real-world models</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The repository provides parsers that extract input features from real-world models and feed them into the trained memory estimator model. The inference for normal and ensemble model are different as their architecture is different.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.5. </span>Considerations for Collecting the data</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow these design considerations both in the data collection scripts and when configuring the launcher script.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Architecture over model types.</span>
To ensure long-term relevance, we focus on architecture families (e.g., CNNs, Transformers) rather than specific models, which quickly become outdated.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Representative and realistic designs.</span>
Synthetic models are generated with feasible architectures (e.g., avoiding excessively deep models) and realistic components such as dropout and batch normalization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diverse and balanced coverage.</span>
We uniformly sample across input features and include varied topologies (e.g., pyramid, hourglass) to promote generalization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input/output variation.</span>
Models include varying input and output dimensions to assess their impact on GPU memory usage.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2. </span>Classification vs. Regression.</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPU memory usage exhibits a staircase-like growth pattern (<a href="#S9.F7" title="In 9. Appendix ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>), observed in our experiments, making regression challenging due to sharp discontinuities, flat plateaus with weak gradients, and spiking errors at step boundaries. These issues lead to instability and overfitting in regression models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17817v1/staricase_growth_pattern.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/156;" width="476" height="156" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>. </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Staircase growth pattern for memory usage, MLPs on ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Russakovsky et al., 2015</a>)</cite> and with batch_size=32.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F4.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.17817v1/MLP_pca3d.png" id="S4.F4.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/380;" width="476" height="380" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S4.F4.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">MLP</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F4.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.17817v1/CNN_pca3d.png" id="S4.F4.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/381;" width="476" height="381" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S4.F4.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">CNN</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F4.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.17817v1/TF_pca3d.png" id="S4.F4.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/382;" width="476" height="382" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.sf3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(c)</span> </span><span id="S4.F4.sf3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Transformer</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>. </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of the dataset across different neural network architectures. The figure shows how discretizing the continuous GPU memory usage facilitates formulating the problem as a classification task.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We formulate the estimation task as classification by discretizing memory usage into fixed-size bins (e.g., 0–1,GB, 1–2,GB). Since CNNs and Transformers exhibit significantly higher memory demands than MLPs, larger bin sizes are used for these architectures to better capture their distribution. Regression models yielded poor performance for both memory and utilization metrics, motivating the use of classification throughout. For GPU utilization metrics, class imbalance and limited coverage of the metric range posed additional challenges, requiring bin adjustments. PCA visualization in <a href="#S4.F4" title="In 4.2. Classification vs. Regression. ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> further reveals that utilization metrics lack clear class separation. This stands in contrast to GPU memory, where more distinct class boundaries are observed—specifically for MLPs—whereas the borders for CNNs and Transformers remain ambiguous, causing the model to become confused when learning these patterns.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3. </span>Selected Features</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For all datasets, the MLP-based estimator uses: <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">batch size</span>, <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">number of parameters</span>, <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">number of activations</span>, <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">#activations <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>
batch size</span> and the
<span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">number of architecture-specific layer types</span> (e.g., linear,
convolutional, batch normalization, and dropout layers). The MLP and CNN datasets
include <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">activation encoding (cos/sin)</span>. The Transformer-based
estimator extends all of the above with a <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">sequence of (layer type,
#activations, #parameters) tuples</span>. These features capture model scale and structure — the primary determinants of GPU memory requirements and utilization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S9.T6" title="In 9. Appendix ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in Appendix presents the target variable ranges alongside total parameters and activations extracted from model summaries. GPU Memory estimator test models are trained with cross-entropy loss (Adam optimizer) and evaluated via stratified 3-fold cross-validation (70% train / 30% validation per fold, with a held-out 30% test set), reporting Accuracy and F1-score to measure overall correctness and class balance, respectively.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">

</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5. </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All data collection and experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA DGX Station A100 equipped with four NVIDIA A100 GPUs (40,GB HBM2 each), using PyTorch 2.4.1 and CUDA 12.2.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6. </span>Evaluation</h2>

<figure id="S6.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17817v1/gpu-ests-comp.svg" id="S6.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/129;" width="476" height="129"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>. </span><span id="S6.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">GPU memory estimation for real-world unseen CNN and Transformer models using Horus, FakeTensor, and GPUMemNet. FakeTensor fails at Transformer models and GPUMemNet cannot estimate for the unseen model, e.g., DLRM (denoted with <span id="S6.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">X</span>). GPUMemNet provides the closest estimations to actual GPU memory consumption and almost never underestimates.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results for the GPU Memory. </span>
GPUMemNet achieves high accuracy on MLPs (serving as a proof-of-concept) and strong performance on CNNs and Transformers (0.81–0.88 at 8 GB memory range bins), supporting the classification formulation for practical memory estimation (<a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.3. Selected Features ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Using an 8 GB bin width preserves accuracy but can limit collocation opportunities, so we experimented with smaller bins. For CNNs and Transformers, however, finer bins degraded performance—reflecting complex, high-variance patterns that would require substantially <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">more data</span> to learn, incurring significant time and hardware costs (a core caveat of data-driven estimation).
A second challenge is drift: any change in frameworks or memory optimizations can invalidate labels, forcing full data recollection and reprocessing.
Third, generalization is brittle: ML estimators extrapolate poorly to unseen architectures or new layers. For example, probing a GPT-2–style model revealed 1D convolution layers—operators absent from GPUMemNet’s Transformer training set—explaining poor extrapolation. This underscores a practical need: keep the GPUMemNet datasets <em id="S6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">open</em> and continuously extended to cover new layers and variants, improving accuracy over time. Finally, the runtime cost of a GPUMemNet estimator model is low: at most <span id="S6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">16 ms</span> on an NVIDIA A100 (40 GB) and <span id="S6.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">32 ms</span> on an AMD EPYC CPU, measured over 100 runs per estimator (<a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.3. Selected Features ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results for the GPU utilization. </span>
Table <a href="#S9.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 9. Appendix ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> in Appendix shows clear performance disparities across architectures. Accuracy drops significantly for non-MLP architectures, with DRAMA scoring as low as 62% on Transformers. Recall — critical for avoiding false low-utilization classifications — is similarly poor across most models. As shown in Figure <a href="#S9.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 9. Appendix ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and discussed in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2. Classification vs. Regression. ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, utilization classes lack clear separation, with CNN and Transformer data points heavily overlapping, hindering meaningful decision boundaries. Furthermore, single-workload utilization prediction assumes additivity, which does not hold due to non-linear inter-workload interactions across execution phases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Memory Estimators on Diverse Real-World Models.</span>

After the in-depth look at the individual strengths and weaknesses of the different GPU memory need estimation methods,
we compare all three estimators—the Horus formula <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeung et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, FakeTensor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite>, and GPUMemNet—on real models in <a href="#S6.F5" title="In 6. Evaluation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
We use GPUMemNet’s MLP-based estimators throughout, given their higher accuracy on CNNs and Transformers (<a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.3. Selected Features ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). The Horus formula can both under- or overestimate—underestimates risk OOM, while overestimates waste memory and reduce collocation. FakeTensor typically underestimates (risking OOM) and, for many Transformer models, produces <em id="S6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">no estimate</em> at all due to unsupported ops.
In contrast, GPUMemNet tends to <em id="S6.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">overestimate</em> memory, reducing potential collocation gains. Its largest error appears on GPT-2—an out-of-distribution case for our training data—where unseen architectural elements drive the mismatch.
Furthermore, it cannot estimate for the DLRM as it has not been trained for it,
underlining the weakness of model-based estimation on unseen cases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Utilization Estimator on Diverse Real-World Models.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S9.T7" title="In 9. Appendix ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> in Appendix reveals clear performance disparities across architectures, with accuracy degrading substantially for non-MLP workloads — DRAMA scores as low as 62% on Transformers. Recall, critical for correctly identifying high-utilization workloads, remains poor across most models. As shown in <a href="#S9.F6" title="In 9. Appendix ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (Appendix) and discussed in <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2. Classification vs. Regression. ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, utilization classes lack clear separability, with CNN and Transformer data points overlapping across all classes, preventing models from learning meaningful decision boundaries. A further limitation is that single-workload prediction implicitly assumes utilization is additive, which does not hold in practice due to non-linear inter-workload interactions from shared GPU resource contention and differing execution phases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7. </span>Discussion and Limitations</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overcoming Limitations of Existing Estimators.</span> Current estimation tools often suffer from intrusive designs that require deep integration into upper software layers, making them impractical for general use. Furthermore, many existing solutions struggle with high latency overhead on the scheduler’s critical path, frequent misestimations, and a general inability to generalize across different models and GPU model heterogeneity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lessons from Initial Experimental Failures.</span> Early attempts using simple MLP datasets revealed that basic models are insufficient for robust prediction. A discrete classifier achieved only <math id="S7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>69% accuracy due to class imbalances, while an <span id="S7.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ExtraTreeRegressor</span> showed poor generalization with a <math id="S7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math>1.2 GB error margin, primarily because it overfitted to a narrow feature set that did not adhere to the principles in <a href="#S4.SS1.SSS5" title="4.1.5. Considerations for Collecting the data ‣ 4.1. Data Collection, Processing, Analysis, and Training Pipeline ‣ 4. Dataset and Problem Formulation ‣ GPU Memory and Utilization Estimation for Training-Aware Resource Management: Opportunities and Limitations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Current Constraints of the GPUMemNet Framework.</span> While <span id="S7.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPUMemNet</span> is effective within its scope, it currently relies on <span id="S7.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torchsummary</span>, which may struggle with custom or non-standard layers. Its performance is tied to training data diversity; without representative data for components like <span id="S7.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Conv1D</span> or residual connections, or support for model/pipeline parallelism, its applicability remains limited to data-parallel setups.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The Challenges of Estimating GPU Utilization.</span> GPU utilization estimation remains an understudied and challenging area where our initial attempts were not successful. Using utilization as a proxy for resource interference is controversial because these metrics are not additive and vary across GPU models, suggesting that future work must address these non-linear hardware complexities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Defining the Path Toward Non-Intrusive Integration.</span> A practical estimator must remain decoupled from specific upper-layer abstractions to support heterogeneous workloads without adding scheduling latency. Ideally, these methods should be integrated directly into ML frameworks, allowing resource metadata to be generated automatically during development without requiring explicit developer intervention.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8. </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we investigated GPU memory and utilization estimation, providing a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative analysis of their respective trade-offs. We presented a data-driven, extensible framework designed to estimate resource requirements for deep learning training tasks. By addressing the practical limitations of current estimation methods, more informed and efficient resource management within GPU clusters can be achieved.</p>
</div>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S9.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>. </span><span id="S9.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Staircase growth pattern for memory usage, MLPs on ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Russakovsky et al., 2015</a>)</cite> and with batch_size=32.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</article>

    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
